newsitem.title: USA: Year-end pressures may cause spike in fed funds.
newsitem.headline: Year-end pressures may cause spike in fed funds.

text.p: It's been more than a decade since the end of the year and the end of a two-week bank maintenance period have fallen on the same date. But market participants should keep in mind that the last time it happened the federal funds rate skyrocketed to 40 percent.

"We haven't had any serious pressures for the last several years. The whole market seems very complacent about yearend and banks are being perhaps a little less cautious than they should be," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at consulting firm MMS International Inc.
Should the federal funds rate spike sharply higher, it probably would not happen until Tuesday, economists said.

"The potential (for a rate spike) is there, but it's not happening right now," Rupert said. She noted that domestic government securities currently were paying only in the 6.5 percent to 7.0 percent range, and much of that trade consisted of swaps with Japanese investors.
Dollar-denominated assets have become more attractive as the currency continues to firm against the yen.
On Friday, the dollar consolidated above 115 yen, its highest level against the Japanese currency in more than three and a half years.
"People on our RP (repurchase agreement) desk are expecting it to be fairly ugly this year," said Joseph Abate, an economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.

Abate noted that the Federal Reserve did not execute a second "coupon pass" to permanently inject reserves into the banking system in late November or early December, as it normally does to address the seasonal add need.

Normally, that would take care of as much as $4.5 billion to $5.0 billion of the Fed's add need. But this year Peter Fisher, head of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's domestic and overseas desks, implied that he did not want to add reserves in November and then have to withdraw them in January, Abate said.

William Sullivan, director of money market research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc, noted that the final six or seven weeks of any calendar year are typically characterized by intense seasonal outflows from the financial system as currency use surges and the reserve requirement of commercial banks balloons -- a development that pulls funds out as well.

Sullivan noted that the Fed did acquire Treasury notes outright during the second week of November for the system account, with the actual pass being a record volume of almost $6.5 billion. However, a second pass never occurred.

Dahlia Harmon, spokeswoman for the New York Fed, said that was in keeping with the Fed's recently announced change in operations whereby coupon passes would be executed over longer periods of time and at different maturity spectrums.
"It gives us the flexibility to move when we see a need out there without having to wait for needs to accumulate to higher levels," she said.
As usual, the Fed would not comment on the possibility of a pass being executed before the end of the year.
Elliott Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, disagreed that the coinciding dates would lead to the heavy pressure experienced in 1985.
"I think the dealers are better positioned this year than they were then," Platt said.

Some economists estimated the Fed's add need could be as high as $14.5 billion in the second week of the current maintenance period. However, it was widely expected the add need would fall off in January.
